The SPA must include a standard net working capital (\"NWC\") true-up mechanism to ensure that the target is delivered to the buyer at closing with a normalized level of working capital. The firm\'s standard NWC adjustment mechanics are as follows:

**Dollar-for-Dollar True-Up.** The NWC adjustment should be a dollar-for-dollar true-up from the first dollar --- i.e., no collar or threshold amount. If the actual NWC at closing exceeds the Target NWC, the purchase price is increased dollar-for-dollar by the excess. If the actual NWC at closing is less than the Target NWC, the purchase price is decreased dollar-for-dollar by the shortfall.

**Target NWC.** The Target NWC should be based on an agreed methodology and should typically reflect the average NWC of the target over the trailing twelve months (or such other period as may be agreed). The methodology for calculating NWC --- including the specific line items included and excluded, the accounting principles to be applied, and any agreed adjustments --- should be set forth in detail in an exhibit to the SPA. A sample NWC calculation based on a recent balance sheet should also be attached to the exhibit to illustrate the methodology.

**Estimated Closing NWC.** The seller must deliver an estimated closing balance sheet and estimated closing NWC calculation to the buyer no later than three (3) business days prior to the scheduled closing date. The estimated closing NWC is used to calculate the purchase price payable at closing, subject to the post-closing true-up.

**Post-Closing True-Up.** Within ninety (90) days following the closing date, the buyer must deliver a final closing balance sheet and final NWC calculation to the seller. The seller has thirty (30) days to review and dispute the buyer\'s calculation. Disputes that cannot be resolved between the parties within fifteen (15) days following the seller\'s objection are submitted to an independent accounting firm (agreed upon by the parties or, failing agreement, selected pursuant to an agreed mechanism) for final, binding resolution. The independent accounting firm\'s determination is limited to the disputed items and must fall within the range defined by the buyer\'s calculation and the seller\'s position. The costs of the independent accounting firm are allocated between the parties based on the relative success of their positions.
**[9.2 Closing Indebtedness and Payoff Letters]{.underline}**

**Firm Standard.** All funded indebtedness of the target must be repaid simultaneously at closing through the closing funds flow. This is a fundamental principle of leveraged acquisition mechanics: the buyer pays a purchase price based on enterprise value, and all existing debt of the target is retired at closing so that the buyer receives the target on a \"cash-free, debt-free\" basis (subject to the NWC adjustment).

The SPA must require the seller to deliver payoff letters from each holder of target indebtedness no later than three (3) business days prior to the scheduled closing date. Each payoff letter must include: (a) the total outstanding balance as of the anticipated closing date (including accrued and unpaid interest, prepayment premiums, breakage costs, and all other amounts necessary to fully satisfy the obligation); (b) wiring instructions for the payoff amount; and (c) an agreement by the lender to deliver lien release documentation (including UCC-3 termination statements, mortgage releases, and intellectual property lien releases, as applicable) promptly upon receipt of the payoff amount.

Delivery of payoff letters meeting these requirements should be a condition to the buyer\'s obligation to close. If payoff letters are not delivered timely, the buyer should have the right to delay closing until they are delivered or, if the delay exceeds a specified number of business days, to terminate the agreement.
**Categories of Indebtedness.** The definition of \"Indebtedness\" in the SPA must be comprehensive and should include all of the following categories:
> \(a\) All obligations for borrowed money, including senior term loans, revolving credit facilities, and subordinated debt (including any seller notes or shareholder loans);
> \(b\) All obligations evidenced by notes, bonds, debentures, or similar instruments;
> \(c\) All capital lease obligations (determined in accordance with GAAP);
> \(d\) All equipment financing obligations;
> \(e\) All guarantees of indebtedness of third parties;
> \(f\) All outstanding letters of credit (to the extent drawn or to the extent backstopped);
> \(g\) All earn-out or deferred purchase price obligations from prior acquisitions by the target;
> \(h\) All accrued and unpaid interest, premiums, penalties, and fees related to any of the foregoing; and
> \(i\) All prepayment penalties, breakage costs, and similar charges payable in connection with the repayment of any of the foregoing.

**Lender Coordination.** The buyer\'s acquisition lender (e.g., Clearwater Environmental Lending Corp. or a similar specialty lender) will typically require payoff letters as a condition to funding the acquisition facility. The SPA\'s closing mechanics must align with the lender\'s requirements regarding the timing and content of payoff letters. Associates should obtain and review the buyer\'s lender\'s commitment letter to identify any specific payoff letter requirements and ensure that the SPA\'s closing conditions are consistent.
**[Section 10: Non-Competition and Non-Solicitation Covenants]{.underline}**
**[10.1 General Standards]{.underline}**

Non-competition and non-solicitation covenants are standard in PE acquisitions and are critical to protecting the buyer\'s investment in the acquired business. A well-drafted non-compete prevents the seller (and its principals) from establishing or participating in a competing business that could divert customers, employees, or business opportunities from the acquired company during the critical post-acquisition integration period.

Associates should always cross-reference the executed term sheet for the agreed-upon non-compete parameters (duration, geographic scope, and business scope). The SPA\'s non-compete provisions must conform to the term sheet.
**Firm Standard for Environmental Services Sector:**

**Duration.** Two (2) to four (4) years post-closing. Three (3) years is the most common duration in recent environmental services transactions handled by the firm and is the firm\'s standard recommendation. Durations shorter than two years provide inadequate protection for the buyer\'s investment; durations longer than four years may raise enforceability concerns in certain jurisdictions.

**Geographic Scope.** The non-compete should be limited to the states and jurisdictions in which the target conducts business as of the closing date, plus any states or jurisdictions in which the target has active proposals or bids pending as of the closing date. A nationwide non-compete is generally not advisable unless the target operates in a majority of states. An overbroad geographic restriction risks unenforceability --- courts in many jurisdictions will decline to enforce a non-compete with a geographic scope that is not reasonably tailored to the legitimate business interest being protected.

**Business Scope.** The non-compete should be limited to the specific business lines of the target --- for example, \"environmental remediation services, hazardous waste management and transportation services, and environmental consulting and engineering services.\" The non-compete should not extend to \"any business\" or to business lines unrelated to the target\'s operations. Where the seller is a diversified holding company with business lines unrelated to the target (e.g., construction, timber management, real estate development), an overbroad non-compete could restrict legitimate seller activities and may be struck down by a court as unreasonable in its scope.

**Enforceability Considerations.** Enforceability of non-compete covenants varies significantly by jurisdiction. Delaware courts generally enforce reasonable non-competition covenants entered into in connection with the sale of a business, applying a reasonableness standard that considers the duration, geographic scope, and business scope of the restriction in light of the legitimate interests being protected. Oregon courts similarly apply a reasonableness test but impose specific statutory requirements for non-compete agreements. Some jurisdictions (most notably California) are hostile to non-compete covenants generally, although the sale-of-business exception may apply. Associates should identify the governing law of the non-compete provision and confirm that the covenant\'s terms are consistent with the requirements of that jurisdiction. Overbroad covenants risk being voided entirely rather than judicially reformed, depending on the jurisdiction\'s approach to reformation (sometimes called \"blue penciling\").

**Non-Solicitation.** In addition to the non-compete, the SPA should include non-solicitation covenants prohibiting the seller and its principals from (a) soliciting or hiring employees of the target and (b) soliciting or diverting customers or suppliers of the target. The non-solicitation period should match the non-compete period.
**[Section 11: Knowledge Qualifiers and Other Definitional Issues]{.underline}**
**[11.1 Knowledge Definition]{.underline}**

The definition of \"Knowledge\" (or \"to the knowledge of the Seller/Company\") is used throughout the SPA to qualify certain representations and warranties. The scope of the Knowledge definition determines whether the seller\'s representations are based solely on the actual awareness of specified individuals or whether they extend to information that such individuals should have known after making reasonable inquiry.

**Firm Standard.** For targets with fewer than 500 employees (which includes the majority of environmental services targets in the middle-market range), actual knowledge of the Chief Executive Officer and Chief Financial Officer (or their functional equivalents) is an acceptable Knowledge standard. These individuals typically have sufficient familiarity with the target\'s operations, financial condition, regulatory compliance status, and material contracts to provide meaningful knowledge-qualified representations.

For targets with more than 500 employees, or for targets with geographically dispersed operations where the CEO and CFO may not have direct visibility into all material matters, a constructive knowledge standard --- knowledge after reasonable inquiry --- applied to a broader group of specified individuals (including, for example, the VP of Operations, the VP of Environmental Compliance, and regional managers) is preferred.

**Note to Associates.** Some associates reflexively mark up knowledge definitions to add constructive knowledge or to expand the list of knowledge individuals in every transaction. For smaller targets where actual knowledge of the CEO and CFO is the standard, this markup is unnecessary and can create unproductive negotiations. Focus your markup efforts on higher-priority items identified in this playbook.
**[11.2 Acceptable Provisions --- When Not to Mark Up]{.underline}**

This section provides guidance on provisions that, while potentially appearing sub-optimal from the buyer\'s perspective, are within acceptable market ranges and should generally NOT be marked up in the seller\'s draft. Disciplined markup is essential to maintaining the credibility of the associate, the responsible partner, and the firm. Marking up provisions that are squarely within market range wastes negotiating capital, creates unnecessary friction, and signals to the seller\'s counsel that the buyer\'s team is either inexperienced or unreasonable.
The following provisions are within the firm\'s acceptable range and should not be marked up absent deal-specific partner instructions to the contrary:

> **Basket/Deductible at 0.75%--1.0% of Enterprise Value.** As discussed in Section 5.2, this is within the firm\'s acceptable range for middle-market environmental services transactions. A basket at 1.0% of enterprise value should not be marked up. Do not attempt to negotiate the basket down to 0.5% or lower merely because a lower basket would be better for the buyer --- the improvement is marginal and the negotiating capital is better spent elsewhere.

> **Knowledge Qualifier Limited to Actual Knowledge of CEO and CFO for Targets Under 500 Employees.** As discussed in Section 11.1, this is the firm\'s accepted standard for smaller targets. Do not mark up the knowledge definition to add constructive knowledge or additional knowledge individuals unless the target has more than 500 employees or the responsible partner instructs otherwise.

> **Good Standing Certificates Dated Within 5--10 Business Days of Closing.** This is the standard timeframe for good standing certificates in M&A transactions. Secretary of state offices in most jurisdictions will issue certificates within this timeframe. Do not mark up a 10-business-day requirement to demand same-day certificates or certificates dated within 3 business days, as this creates logistical complications without meaningful benefit.

> **Delaware Governing Law.** Delaware is the preferred governing law for SPAs in transactions where both the buyer and the seller have connections to Delaware (e.g., where one or both parties are Delaware entities). Delaware\'s well-developed body of corporate and contract law, sophisticated judiciary, and predictable outcomes make it an optimal choice. Do not mark up a Delaware governing law clause to substitute another jurisdiction\'s law absent specific instructions from the responsible partner.

**General Principle.** The associate\'s credibility --- and the firm\'s reputation --- depends on disciplined, strategic markup. Do not mark up provisions that are within market range merely to demonstrate thoroughness or to generate a longer redline. Focus markup energy exclusively on provisions that (i) deviate from the executed term sheet, (ii) violate the requirements set forth in this playbook, or (iii) expose the buyer to material uncompensated risk. Every markup should be defensible with reference to the term sheet, this playbook, or a specific risk identified in due diligence.
**[Section 12: Environmental Regulatory Considerations (Sector-Specific)]{.underline}**
**[12.1 Environmental Permit Transfers]{.underline}**

In a stock acquisition, the target entity itself does not change --- the same legal entity that held the environmental permits before the transaction continues to hold them after the transaction. This is one of the principal advantages of a stock purchase structure for environmental services targets with complex permitting portfolios. However, the mere fact that the permit-holding entity does not change does not mean that the change of control is transparent to regulators.

Many state environmental regulatory programs --- including programs authorized under RCRA, the Clean Air Act, and the Clean Water Act --- require notification to, or approval from, the issuing regulatory agency upon a change of control of the permit holder, even in stock purchase transactions. The specific requirements vary by state and by permit type, and failure to comply with applicable notification or approval requirements can result in permit violations, enforcement actions, or, in extreme cases, permit revocation.

**States of Particular Note.** Based on the firm\'s recent transaction experience in the environmental services sector, the following states impose change-of-control notification or approval requirements that are particularly relevant:

> \(a\) **Oregon:** The Oregon Department of Environmental Quality (\"DEQ\") requires change-of-ownership notifications for certain categories of environmental permits, including RCRA hazardous waste facility permits and water quality permits.
> \(b\) **Washington:** The Washington Department of Ecology requires similar notifications and, in some cases, formal approval for changes of ownership affecting certain environmental permits.

> \(c\) **California:** The California Department of Toxic Substances Control (\"DTSC\") has specific requirements for notification and, in certain circumstances, prior approval of changes of control for hazardous waste facility permits.
> \(d\) **Nevada:** The Nevada Division of Environmental Protection (\"NDEP\") imposes change-of-ownership notification requirements for certain permits.

**Firm Standard.** The SPA should include both (a) a representation regarding the current status of all Environmental Permits held by the target (including confirmation that all permits are in full force and effect, that no permit is subject to pending revocation or suspension, and that no conditions exist that could give rise to revocation or suspension) AND (b) pre-closing and post-closing covenants requiring the seller\'s cooperation in the notification, transfer, or re-issuance of Environmental Permits as required by applicable law. The cooperation covenant should extend through a period of at least twelve (12) months post-closing to cover permits with longer regulatory processing timelines.

Associates should review the environmental due diligence memo for a comprehensive list of all target permits and should flag any permits that require transfer notifications or regulatory approvals in connection with the change of control.
**[12.2 Government Contract Considerations]{.underline}**

Environmental services companies frequently derive a significant portion of their revenue from government contracts --- including federal, state, and local contracts --- for environmental remediation, environmental consulting, environmental monitoring, and related services. Government contracts present unique legal issues in the acquisition context that associates must address in the SPA.

**Federal Government Contracts.** Federal government contracts are subject to the Anti-Assignment Act (41 U.S.C. § 6305), which generally prohibits the assignment of government contracts without the consent of the contracting officer. In addition, FAR 42.12 sets forth the procedures for novation agreements when a contractor undergoes a change of ownership. A novation agreement is a three-party agreement among the government, the original contractor, and the successor contractor, pursuant to which the government recognizes the successor as the contractor under the existing contract.

Even in stock purchase transactions --- where the contracting entity does not change --- certain changes in ownership may trigger novation or recognition requirements under FAR. Specifically, FAR 42.1204 provides that a novation agreement may be required when a contractor is acquired by another entity, even if the contractor entity continues to exist. The determination of whether a novation is required depends on the circumstances, including whether the contractor entity remains intact and continues to perform under the contract.
**Firm Standard.** The SPA should include:

> \(i\) A representation regarding the status of all government contracts held by the target, including confirmation that all contracts are in good standing, that no contracts are subject to pending termination for default or convenience, and that no debarment or suspension proceedings are pending or threatened;

> \(ii\) A pre-closing covenant requiring the seller and the target to use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain novation or recognition agreements from applicable government contracting officers, to the extent required by applicable law or regulation; and

> \(iii\) Consideration of whether government contract consent should be a closing condition. For targets where government contracts represent a material portion of revenue (typically more than 20%), the failure to obtain required novation agreements may justify a closing condition. For targets with a smaller government contract exposure, a pre-closing covenant with commercially reasonable efforts may be sufficient.

Associates should cross-reference the government contracts section of the due diligence memo and consult with the firm\'s Government Contracts Practice Group for guidance on specific novation requirements.
**[Section 13: Closing Conditions]{.underline}**
**[13.1 Standard Buyer Closing Conditions]{.underline}**
The SPA must include the following standard closing conditions for the buyer\'s benefit. These conditions are required in every PE acquisition SPA and should not be omitted or materially diluted:

> \(a\) **Accuracy of Representations and Warranties.** The seller\'s representations and warranties must be true and correct as of the closing date as though made on such date (with appropriate exceptions for representations made as of a specific date). For non-Fundamental Representations, accuracy is qualified by a Material Adverse Effect standard (i.e., the representations must be true and correct except where the failure to be true and correct would not, individually or in the aggregate, reasonably be expected to have a Material Adverse Effect). For Fundamental Representations, accuracy must be true and correct in all respects (other than de minimis inaccuracies).

> \(b\) **Compliance with Covenants.** The seller and the target must have complied in all material respects with all covenants and agreements required to be performed by them at or prior to the closing.
> \(c\) **No Material Adverse Effect.** No Material Adverse Effect shall have occurred since the date of the agreement.
> \(d\) **HSR Act Clearance.** If the transaction is reportable under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Antitrust Improvements Act of 1976, all applicable waiting periods shall have expired or been terminated.

> \(e\) **Third-Party Consents.** All consents required for the assignment or transfer of material contracts (including material customer contracts, material supplier contracts, and material leases) shall have been obtained.
> \(f\) **Delivery of Payoff Letters.** Payoff letters from all holders of target indebtedness shall have been delivered in accordance with the SPA\'s requirements (see Section 9.2).
> \(g\) **Officer\'s Certificate.** An officer of the seller or the target shall have delivered a certificate certifying the satisfaction of the conditions set forth in clauses (a) through (c) above.

> \(h\) **Secretary\'s Certificate.** The secretary (or equivalent officer) of the target shall have delivered a certificate attaching the target\'s organizational documents, resolutions authorizing the transaction, and incumbency of officers.

> \(i\) **Good Standing Certificates.** Good standing certificates (or certificates of existence, as applicable) for the target from its jurisdiction of organization and each jurisdiction in which it is qualified to do business, dated within ten (10) business days of the closing date.
> \(j\) **Employment and Non-Compete Agreements.** Executed employment agreements and/or non-competition agreements with key employees identified in the SPA or the term sheet.

> \(k\) **FIRPTA Certificate.** A certificate from the seller meeting the requirements of Treasury Regulations Section 1.1445-2(b)(2), certifying that the seller is not a foreign person for purposes of FIRPTA.
> \(l\) **R&W Insurance Policy.** If the buyer is obtaining R&W Insurance, evidence that the R&W Insurance policy has been bound and is in full force and effect.

> \(m\) **No Injunctions.** No temporary restraining order, preliminary or permanent injunction, or other order or decree issued by any court of competent jurisdiction or governmental authority shall be in effect that prevents or prohibits the consummation of the transactions contemplated by the agreement.
**[13.2 Sector-Specific Closing Conditions]{.underline}**
In addition to the standard closing conditions set forth in Section 13.1, the following sector-specific closing conditions should be included in environmental services acquisitions where applicable:

> \(a\) **Government Contract Novation or Recognition.** Where the target holds material government contracts that require novation or recognition agreements in connection with the change of control, the receipt of such novation or recognition agreements (or, at minimum, written confirmation from the applicable contracting officer that the novation process is underway and that interim performance will be permitted) should be a closing condition. See Section 12.2 for further guidance.

> \(b\) **Environmental Permit Transfer Notifications.** Where applicable state law requires notification to or approval from a regulatory agency in connection with a change of control of the permit holder, confirmation that all required notifications have been filed (and, where prior approval is required, that such approval has been obtained) should be a closing condition. See Section 12.1 for further guidance.

> \(c\) **No New Environmental Claims.** Confirmation that no new material environmental claim, enforcement action, notice of violation, CERCLA information request, or similar regulatory action has been received by the target since the date of the agreement that would, individually or in the aggregate, reasonably be expected to have a Material Adverse Effect.

> \(d\) **Environmental Impairment Liability Insurance.** Confirmation that all environmental impairment liability insurance policies maintained by the target remain in full force and effect as of the closing date, with coverage levels no less than those in effect as of the date of the agreement.
**[Section 14: Checklist Summary --- Key Markup Items for Environmental Services SPAs]{.underline}**

The following checklist summarizes all critical and high-priority items covered in this playbook. Associates should use this checklist as a quick-reference guide when performing markup of a seller\'s draft SPA in an environmental services transaction. Each item includes a priority designation and a cross-reference to the relevant section of this playbook for detailed guidance.

1\. **MAE Definition --- Disproportionate Impact Qualifier** \[CRITICAL\]. Confirm that all industry-specific and regulatory carve-outs in the MAE definition include a \"disproportionate impact\" qualifier. If the carve-out for \"changes in the environmental services industry generally\" or \"changes in environmental laws or regulations\" lacks the qualifier, flag and correct immediately. *(Ref. Section 2.1)*

2\. **Interim Covenants --- Affiliate Transaction Restriction** \[HIGH\]. Confirm that the interim operating covenants include a specific restriction prohibiting the target from entering into, amending, extending, or terminating any affiliate transaction without buyer\'s prior written consent. *(Ref. Section 3.2)*

3\. **Indemnification Cap --- Conformity with Term Sheet** \[CRITICAL\]. Confirm that the general indemnification cap matches the percentage agreed in the executed term sheet (typical range: 10%--15% of enterprise value; firm standard: 12.5%). Flag and correct any deviation from the term sheet. *(Ref. Section 5.1)*

4\. **Environmental Representation Survival --- Minimum 36 Months** \[CRITICAL\]. Confirm that environmental representations survive for a minimum of 36 months post-closing, carved out from the general representation survival period. Preferred position: full statute of limitations. *(Ref. Section 4.2)*

5\. **Pro-Sandbagging Clause** \[CRITICAL\]. Confirm that the SPA contains an affirmative pro-sandbagging provision. If the seller\'s draft contains an anti-sandbagging clause, strike it and replace with pro-sandbagging language. *(Ref. Section 5.3)*

6\. **Special Indemnity for Known Environmental Liabilities** \[CRITICAL\]. Confirm that a Special Indemnity is included for each identified environmental liability with estimated exposure of \$1,000,000 or more; 72-month survival; dollar-one recovery (outside the basket); not subject to the general cap. *(Ref. Section 6)*

7\. **Earnout Operational Covenants --- No Affirmative Obligations** \[HIGH\]. Confirm that earnout provisions do not contain affirmative operational covenants (e.g., \"operate in a manner consistent with past practice\" or \"maximize the Earnout Payment\"). Only the narrow \"primary purpose\" negative covenant is acceptable. *(Ref. Section 7.2)*
8\. **R&W Insurance Subrogation Waiver** \[HIGH\]. Confirm that the SPA includes a waiver of the R&W insurer\'s subrogation rights against the seller (except for fraud). *(Ref. Section 8.2)*

9\. **Payoff Letters as Closing Condition** \[HIGH\]. Confirm that the SPA requires delivery of payoff letters from all holders of target indebtedness at least 3 business days prior to closing, and that delivery is a condition to buyer\'s obligation to close. *(Ref. Section 9.2)*

10\. **Non-Compete Scope** \[MEDIUM-HIGH\]. Confirm that non-compete provisions match the term sheet in duration, geographic scope, and business scope. Avoid overbroad restrictions that could capture seller\'s unrelated business activities or that risk unenforceability. *(Ref. Section 10.1)*

11\. **Government Contract Novation** \[HIGH\]. Confirm that the SPA addresses Anti-Assignment Act and FAR novation requirements, including representations, pre-closing covenants, and (where applicable) closing conditions for material government contracts. *(Ref. Section 12.2)*

12\. **Environmental Permit Transfer Covenants** \[HIGH\]. Confirm that the SPA includes cooperation covenants for environmental permit notifications and transfers required by applicable state law in connection with the change of control. *(Ref. Section 12.1)*

13\. **Do Not Mark Up** \[GUIDANCE\]. The following items are within acceptable market range and should generally not be marked up: basket/deductible at 0.75%--1.0% of enterprise value; actual knowledge of CEO and CFO for targets with fewer than 500 employees; good standing certificates dated within 5--10 business days of closing; Delaware governing law. *(Ref. Section 11.2)*

(\"Cascadia\" or the \"Company\"), an Oregon corporation headquartered at 8700 SW Tualatin-Sherwood Road, Suite 200, Tualatin, Oregon 97062. The Company employs approximately 340 full-time employees across these operations.
Line 27: 1\. **Dalton Creek CERCLA Exposure (HIGH RISK).** The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has issued an information request under CERCLA § 104(e) to Cascadia regarding the Company\'s former operations at the Dalton Creek disposal facility. Although no formal enforcement action or PRP designation has been issued to date, the § 104(e) letter is a well-recognized precursor to potential enforcement activity. We estimate Cascadia\'s potential liability exposure in the range of \$1,500,000 to \$6,000,000, depending upon EPA\'s cost allocation approach and the solvency of other potentially responsible parties.
Line 29: 2\. **Hargrove Industrial Site Remediation (MODERATE RISK).** Cascadia is actively performing environmental remediation at the former Hargrove Industrial Site in Milwaukie, Oregon, under contract with the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality. Estimated remaining remediation costs total approximately \$4,200,000. This exposure is a contractual obligation and is covered by a site-specific environmental liability insurance policy with a \$10,000,000 policy limit, which appears adequate.
Line 47: > • **CERCLA Correspondence.** The EPA\'s CERCLA § 104(e) information request regarding the Dalton Creek disposal facility, dated February 12, 2025, together with the Company\'s written response thereto and all related internal correspondence and records.

Line 67: Cascadia formerly operated at the Dalton Creek disposal facility, a former hazardous waste disposal site located in Clackamas County, Oregon. The Company\'s operations at Dalton Creek involved the handling, treatment, and disposal of hazardous wastes generated by third-party industrial customers. These operations significantly predate the current management team and were conducted during a period when the Company was under different operational leadership. According to records produced during due diligence and confirmed by management interviews, Cascadia ceased all operations at the Dalton Creek disposal facility in approximately 2015.
Line 75: Based on our review of the Company\'s records, the EPA information request and the Company\'s response, publicly available site information, and consultation with environmental counsel experienced in CERCLA cost allocation proceedings, we estimate Cascadia\'s potential liability exposure in connection with the Dalton Creek disposal facility to be in the range of **\$1,500,000 to \$6,000,000**. Under this scenario, Cascadia\'s share would represent a minority allocation consistent with its relative contribution to site contamination.

Under CERCLA § 107, liability is joint and several, meaning that EPA may seek recovery of the full cost of remediation from any single PRP, regardless of that party\'s proportionate contribution. If other PRPs are insolvent or unidentifiable, Cascadia\'s exposure could increase significantly. The high-end estimate also accounts for the possibility that the overall scope and cost of site remediation may exceed current projections.

matches.line: Ashford, Pennington & Yates LLP\'s Environmental Practice Group has completed its environmental due diligence review of Cascadia Environmental Solutions, Inc. (\"Cascadia\" or the \"Company\"), an Oregon corporation headquartered at 8700 SW Tualatin-Sherwood Road, Suite 200, Tualatin, Oregon 97062. Cascadia provides environmental remediation, hazardous waste management, and environmental consulting services, operating through seven offices located in Oregon, Washington, California, and Nevada. The Company employs approximately 340 full-time employees across these operations.

1\. **Dalton Creek CERCLA Exposure (HIGH RISK).** The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has issued an information request under CERCLA § 104(e) to Cascadia regarding the Company\'s former operations at the Dalton Creek disposal facility. Although no formal enforcement action or PRP designation has been issued to date, the § 104(e) letter is a well-recognized precursor to potential enforcement activity. We estimate Cascadia\'s potential liability exposure in the range of \$1,500,000 to \$6,000,000, depending upon EPA\'s cost allocation approach and the solvency of other potentially responsible parties.

2\. **Hargrove Industrial Site Remediation (MODERATE RISK).** Cascadia is actively performing environmental remediation at the former Hargrove Industrial Site in Milwaukie, Oregon, under contract with the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality. Estimated remaining remediation costs total approximately \$4,200,000. This exposure is a contractual obligation and is covered by a site-specific environmental liability insurance policy with a \$10,000,000 policy limit, which appears adequate.

> • **CERCLA Correspondence.** The EPA\'s CERCLA § 104(e) information request regarding the Dalton Creek disposal facility, dated February 12, 2025, together with the Company\'s written response thereto and all related internal correspondence and records.

> • **Remediation Contracts.** All remediation contracts, statements of work, and work plans pertaining to the Hargrove Industrial Site remediation project, including the master contract with the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality and applicable task orders.

> • **Insurance Policies.** Environmental impairment liability insurance policies issued by Northshore Specialty Insurance Co. to the Company, including the general environmental impairment liability policy (aggregate limit of \$15,000,000; per-occurrence limit of \$5,000,000) and the site-specific environmental liability insurance policy covering the Hargrove Industrial Site (policy limit of \$10,000,000).

Cascadia formerly operated at the Dalton Creek disposal facility, a former hazardous waste disposal site located in Clackamas County, Oregon. The Company\'s operations at Dalton Creek involved the handling, treatment, and disposal of hazardous wastes generated by third-party industrial customers. These operations significantly predate the current management team and were conducted during a period when the Company was under different operational leadership. According to records produced during due diligence and confirmed by management interviews, Cascadia ceased all operations at the Dalton Creek disposal facility in approximately 2015.

Based on our review of the Company\'s records, the EPA information request and the Company\'s response, publicly available site information, and consultation with environmental counsel experienced in CERCLA cost allocation proceedings, we estimate Cascadia\'s potential liability exposure in connection with the Dalton Creek disposal facility to be in the range of **\$1,500,000 to \$6,000,000**. The factors underlying this range are as follows:

> • **Low End (\$1,500,000).** This estimate assumes that EPA pursues a multi-party cost allocation among all identified potentially responsible parties at the Dalton Creek site, that Cascadia\'s proportionate share of total cleanup costs is determined on the basis of the volume and toxicity of waste it disposed at the facility, and that other identified PRPs remain solvent and capable of bearing their respective shares. Under this scenario, Cascadia\'s share would represent a minority allocation consistent with its relative contribution to site contamination.

> • **High End (\$6,000,000).** This estimate reflects the possibility that EPA may designate Cascadia as a major contributor to the contamination at the site, or that one or more other PRPs may prove financially unable to satisfy their allocated shares. Under CERCLA § 107, liability is joint and several, meaning that EPA may seek recovery of the full cost of remediation from any single PRP, regardless of that party\'s proportionate contribution. If other PRPs are insolvent or unidentifiable, Cascadia\'s exposure could increase significantly. The high-end estimate also accounts for the possibility that the overall scope and cost of site remediation may exceed current projections.

**Recommendation 1 --- Special Indemnity.** Given the magnitude of the potential exposure (\$1,500,000 to \$6,000,000), the fact that this is a known and disclosed environmental liability arising from Seller\'s period of ownership, and the inherent uncertainty and protracted timeline of CERCLA proceedings, we **strongly recommend** that the SPA include a **Special Indemnity** obligating Seller to indemnify Buyer for all Losses arising from or related to the Dalton Creek disposal facility and the EPA\'s CERCLA § 104(e) information request, including without limitation all costs of investigation, remediation, defense, settlement, contribution, and related administrative proceedings. The Special Indemnity should be structured as follows:

> \(c\) **Escrow Holdback.** The Special Indemnity should be supported by a dedicated portion of the **escrow holdback** maintained with Pinnacle Trust Company for a minimum period of **36 months** following closing. The escrowed amount should be sufficient to cover at least the low end of the estimated liability range (\$1,500,000), with the full Special Indemnity obligation surviving for the 72-month period regardless of the release of escrowed funds.

> \(b\) Cascadia\'s active remediation projects, including the Hargrove Industrial Site project, have multi-year performance timelines during which new environmental liabilities or breaches of environmental representations may emerge.
**[IV. Hargrove Industrial Site Remediation]{.underline}**

Cascadia is currently performing active environmental remediation at the former Hargrove Industrial Site, located in Milwaukie, Oregon, under a remediation services contract with the Oregon Department of Environmental Quality (\"Oregon DEQ\"). The Hargrove project involves soil and groundwater remediation activities at the former industrial site, including excavation and off-site disposal of contaminated soil, installation and operation of a groundwater extraction and treatment system, and ongoing environmental monitoring. The Company estimates the total remaining cost to complete the remediation at approximately **\$4,200,000**, with the project expected to continue for approximately 18 to 24 months beyond the anticipated closing date. The Hargrove remediation contract is one of the Company\'s four active government contracts and represents a significant ongoing commitment of Company resources and personnel.

Cascadia carries a site-specific environmental liability insurance policy issued by **Northshore Specialty Insurance Co.** with a **\$10,000,000 policy limit** specifically covering the Hargrove Industrial Site remediation project. This policy provides coverage for remediation costs, cost overruns, and third-party claims arising from the Company\'s remediation activities at the Hargrove site. Separately, the Company\'s broader environmental impairment liability insurance with Northshore Specialty Insurance Co. carries an aggregate limit of \$15,000,000 and a per-occurrence limit of \$5,000,000. The site-specific Hargrove policy appears adequate to cover the estimated remaining \$4,200,000 remediation cost plus potential cost overruns and third-party claims, assuming no policy exclusions or coverage defenses are applicable. We recommend that the SPA include a representation that all environmental insurance policies maintained by the Company are in full force and effect, that all premiums due have been paid, and that no notice of cancellation, non-renewal, or material modification has been received. The SPA should also include a pre-closing covenant requiring the Company to maintain all such policies through and following the closing date.

We assess the Hargrove Industrial Site remediation project as a **moderate risk** item. The project is a standard remediation engagement being performed under a government contract with the Oregon DEQ. The principal risks are (i) cost overruns in excess of the current \$4,200,000 estimate, (ii) potential regulatory enforcement action if the Company fails to meet remediation milestones established in the work plan and consent order, and (iii) third-party claims arising from remediation activities. The available insurance coverage appears adequate to mitigate these risks. We note that the Oregon DEQ contract under which the Hargrove work is being performed is one of the four government contracts requiring novation or consent analysis, as discussed in Section VI below.

> • **Oregon.** Oregon DEQ regulations require notification of a change of ownership or control of a permitted facility within 30 days of such change. Certain RCRA permits issued by Oregon DEQ may require formal transfer approval prior to the change taking effect. *See* OAR Chapter 340, Division 012 and applicable permit conditions.
> 1\. **Oregon Department of Environmental Quality** --- Environmental remediation services, including the Hargrove Industrial Site remediation project discussed in Section IV above.

**Hargrove Site-Specific Policy.** In addition to the general EIL policy, the Company maintains a project-specific environmental liability policy covering the Hargrove Industrial Site remediation project. This policy carries a \$10,000,000 policy limit and provides coverage for remediation costs, cost overruns, and third-party claims arising specifically from the Company\'s remediation activities at the Hargrove site.

> • **Insurance Maintenance Covenant.** SPA should include a pre-closing covenant requiring the Company to maintain all environmental insurance policies (EIL and Hargrove site-specific) in full force and effect through closing, with a representation that all premiums have been paid and no notice of cancellation has been received.

{"file_path":"memo.md","content":"# PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT

## Markup Memorandum — Cascadia Environmental Solutions, Inc. Stock Purchase Agreement

**To:** Elena Vasquez-Moreno, Partner, M&A Group; Jonathan Kreider, Senior Associate, M&A Group  
**From:** Buyer-side deal team  
**Date:** October 29, 2025  
**Re:** Whitmore Capital Partners LLC acquisition of Cascadia Environmental Solutions, Inc. — review of Seller's draft SPA  
**Status:** Buyer-side markup memorandum; draft-ready language for negotiation with Fortuna & Blake LLP

## 1. Executive summary

Seller's October 22, 2025 draft is materially seller-favorable and departs from the September 10, 2025 executed term sheet in several binding economic and risk-allocation provisions. The most important changes are: (i) adding the required disproportionate-impact qualifiers to the MAE carve-outs; (ii) removing the anti-sandbagging clause; (iii) replacing the affirmative earnout operating covenant with the agreed primary-purpose standard; (iv) adding a Dalton Creek Special Indemnity; (v) correcting the general indemnification cap from $43,000,000 (20%) to $26,875,000 (12.5%); (vi) extending environmental representation survival to at least 36 months; (vii) adding government-contract novation/recognition covenants and an appropriately calibrated closing condition; (viii) adding environmental permit change-of-control cooperation; (ix) making payoff letters and simultaneous debt payoff a closing condition/mechanic; (x) adding the R&W insurance subrogation waiver; and (xi) narrowing the non-compete and non-solicitation covenants to the term-sheet scope.

This memorandum is organized by SPA article/section. For each issue, the memorandum provides the Seller's language, a complete proposed replacement or insertion, a track-changes-style comment, priority, and cross-references to the executed term sheet, the buyer M&A playbook, the environmental DD memo, and the partner's instructions.

### Priority legend

- **Critical:** must be corrected before approval of the buyer's markup; a term-sheet deviation or material risk allocation.
- **High:** material protection required by the playbook or diligence; do not concede without partner/client approval.
- **Medium:** important drafting or scope correction; commercially defensible and should be included in the first markup.

## 2. Issues that should not be marked up

The following Seller provisions are acceptable and should be left unchanged unless a new fact develops:

1. **Basket/deductible:** $2,150,000, equal to 1% of Base Enterprise Value, expressly a true deductible. This is within the playbook's 0.75%–1.0% range and matches the term sheet.
2. **Knowledge qualifier:** actual knowledge of Patricia Huang and Robert Merrill. Cascadia has approximately 340 employees, so this is within the playbook's accepted standard for targets under 500 employees.
3. **Good-standing certificates:** no more than 10 days before Closing. This is within the playbook's 5–10 business-day range.
4. **Delaware governing law:** appropriate because Buyer and Seller are Delaware entities and consistent with the term sheet/playbook.
5. **NWC true-up mechanics:** dollar-for-dollar, no collar, 90-day Buyer statement, Seller review, and independent accountant dispute resolution are generally consistent with the term sheet and playbook. The payoff and funds-flow mechanics, however, require the revisions below.

# ARTICLE I — DEFINITIONS

## 3. Section 1.01 — Material Adverse Effect: disproportionate-impact qualifiers

**Priority: Critical**

### Seller's draft language

> “(ii) changes in conditions generally affecting the environmental services industry; (iii) changes in Environmental Laws or regulations;”

### Proposed replacement language

Replace clauses (ii) and (iii) of the definition of “Material Adverse Effect” with the following, and add the final proviso to the carve-out paragraph:

> “(ii) changes in conditions generally affecting the environmental services industry; (iii) changes in Environmental Laws or regulations; ... provided, however, that any change, effect, event, development, state of facts, condition, circumstance, or occurrence referred to in clauses (i) through (viii) above shall be taken into account in determining whether a Material Adverse Effect has occurred or would reasonably be expected to occur to the extent such change, effect, event, development, state of facts, condition, circumstance, or occurrence disproportionately affects the Company relative to other participants in the environmental services industry or other similarly situated participants in the industries in which the Company operates.”

For clarity, the complete carve-out paragraph should read:

> “provided, however, that none of the following, individually or in the aggregate, shall be deemed to constitute, or shall be taken into account in determining whether there has been or would reasonably be expected to be, a Material Adverse Effect: (i) changes in general economic, financial, credit, securities market, or political conditions in the United States or globally; (ii) changes in conditions generally affecting the environmental services industry; (iii) changes in Environmental Laws or regulations; (iv) changes in GAAP or applicable Law (other than Environmental Laws, which are addressed in clause (iii) above); (v) acts of war, armed hostilities, sabotage, terrorism, military actions, or any escalation or worsening thereof, epidemics, pandemics, earthquakes, hurricanes, tornados, floods, or other natural disasters or acts of God; (vi) the announcement or pendency of the transactions contemplated by this Agreement, including any impact on relationships with customers, suppliers, employees, or Governmental Authorities; (vii) any action taken by the Company at the express written request or with the express written consent of Buyer; and (viii) any failure by the Company to meet any internal or external projections, forecasts, or estimates of revenue, earnings, or other financial performance metrics for any period (provided that the underlying facts, circumstances, and causes of any such failure may be considered in determining whether a Material Adverse Effect has occurred); provided, further, that any change, effect, event, development, state of facts, condition, circumstance, or occurrence referred to in clauses (i) through (viii) above shall be taken into account in determining whether a Material Adverse Effect has occurred or would reasonably be expected to occur to the extent such change, effect, event, development, state of facts, condition, circumstance, or occurrence disproportionately affects the Company relative to other participants in the environmental services industry or other similarly situated participants in the industries in which the Company operates.”

### Track-changes comment

**[Buyer comment — CRITICAL: restore agreed MAE protection.]** The Seller's unqualified industry and Environmental Law carve-outs could exclude the very regulatory or sector-specific developments most likely to impair Cascadia. Add the disproportionate-impact qualifier required by Playbook Sections 2.1–2.2 and checklist item 1. The qualifier is also necessary because the DD memo identifies a highly regulated permit portfolio and a pending CERCLA information request. The provision should not allow a target-specific regulatory development or enforcement initiative to be treated as an excluded industry-wide event.

**Sources:** Buyer M&A Playbook §§2.1–2.2; Partner Instructions ¶¶52–67; DD Memo §§III, V; term-sheet §12 (Buyer closing condition for no MAE).

## 4. Section 1.01 — Adjusted EBITDA: add-backs and mechanics

**Priority: Medium**

### Seller's draft language

> “Adjusted EBITDA” means ... net income ... plus (a) interest expense, (b) income tax expense, and (c) depreciation and amortization expense ... and further adjusted to exclude (i) non-recurring transaction costs ... (ii) purchase-price accounting adjustments ... (iii) extraordinary or non-recurring items, and (iv) management fees, monitoring fees, or similar fees charged by Buyer or any of its Affiliates ... The detailed calculation methodology ... is set forth on Exhibit D.

### Proposed replacement language

Replace the definition with:

> “Adjusted EBITDA” means, with respect to the Measurement Period, the net income of the Company for such period determined in accordance with GAAP applied consistently with the Company’s past practice, plus, to the extent deducted in computing such net income, (a) interest expense, (b) income tax expense, and (c) depreciation and amortization expense, and further adjusted to exclude or add back, without duplication: (i) all transaction-related fees, costs, and expenses incurred in connection with the transactions contemplated by this Agreement, including legal, accounting, advisory, financing, and diligence fees; (ii) all purchase-price accounting adjustments arising from the transactions contemplated hereby; (iii) all Buyer-directed integration costs, restructuring charges, and other one-time costs incurred after Closing in connection with integrating, reorganizing, or restructuring the Company; (iv) all non-recurring or extraordinary items, including one-time litigation costs, regulatory penalties, and extraordinary expenses; (v) corporate overhead allocations charged by Buyer or any Affiliate of Buyer that were not charged to the Company on a consistent basis before Closing; (vi) intercompany charges from Buyer or any Affiliate of Buyer that were not charged to the Company on a consistent basis before Closing; (vii) management fees, monitoring fees, or similar fees charged by Buyer or any Affiliate of Buyer; and (viii) the excess, if any, of rent and related occupancy costs payable under the Affiliate Lease over the fair-market rent for the applicable premises, in each case as reflected in Exhibit D. No item shall be added back more than once, and no adjustment shall be made for any item that is already reflected in the calculation of the Purchase Price or otherwise results in duplication of recovery.”

### Track-changes comment

The thresholds and formula in Sections 2.05(a)–(b) correctly match the term sheet, but the definition should expressly address Buyer-directed integration/restructuring costs, unhistorical corporate allocations, and affiliate charges. The Seller's draft already excludes Buyer affiliate management fees, but the broader drafting above avoids disputes over the exact form of post-Closing cost allocations and captures the $1,600,000 Affiliate Lease issue identified in the partner instructions and disclosure schedules.

**Sources:** Term Sheet §5; Playbook §§7.1–7.2; Partner Instructions ¶¶107–111 and ¶¶182–191; Seller Disclosure Schedule 4.21.

## 5. Section 1.01 — Indemnification Cap

**Priority: Critical**

### Seller's draft language

> “Indemnification Cap” means Forty-Three Million Dollars ($43,000,000), which is equal to twenty percent (20%) of the Base Enterprise Value.

### Proposed replacement language

> “Indemnification Cap” means Twenty-Six Million Eight Hundred Seventy-Five Thousand Dollars ($26,875,000), which is equal to twelve and one-half percent (12.5%) of the Base Enterprise Value. For the avoidance of doubt, the Indemnification Cap shall apply to aggregate Losses arising from breaches of non-Fundamental Representations and shall not apply to the Dalton Creek Special Indemnity, breaches of Fundamental Representations, or fraud or willful misconduct, in each case as expressly provided in Article IX.

### Track-changes comment

**[Buyer comment — CRITICAL: binding economic term.]** The $43,000,000 cap is a direct departure from the binding term-sheet cap of 12.5% of $215,000,000, or $26,875,000. R&W Insurance does not justify changing the agreed SPA cap. Correct the defined term and conform Section 9.04(b).

**Sources:** Term Sheet §§8 and 18(iv); Playbook §5.1 and checklist item 3; Partner Instructions ¶¶143–154.

# ARTICLE II — PURCHASE AND SALE; PURCHASE PRICE

## 6. Section 2.05 — Earnout operating covenant and payment mechanics

**Priority: Critical**

### Seller's draft language

> “From and after the Closing Date through the end of the Earnout Period, Buyer shall, and shall cause the Company to, operate the business of the Company in a manner consistent with past practice and in good faith to maximize the Earnout Payment. Without limiting the foregoing, Buyer shall not, and shall cause the Company not to, take any action that would reasonably be expected to reduce the Adjusted EBITDA of the Company below the levels that would otherwise have been achieved. In furtherance of the foregoing, during the Earnout Period, Buyer shall cause the Company to maintain substantially the same level of personnel, equipment, and other resources as in effect immediately prior to the Closing Date and shall not divert or redirect any contracts, customers, revenues, or business opportunities of the Company to Buyer or any of its Affiliates.”

The Seller's draft also provides for an Earnout Statement within 60 days after the end of the Earnout Period and payment within 10 Business Days after final determination.

### Proposed replacement language

Replace Sections 2.05(c), 2.05(d), and 2.05(e) with:

> **(c) Earnout Calculation and Dispute Resolution.** Within forty-five (45) days after the end of the Earnout Period, Buyer shall prepare and deliver to Seller a written statement (the “Earnout Statement”) setting forth Buyer’s good-faith calculation of Adjusted EBITDA for the Earnout Period and the resulting Earnout Payment, if any, together with reasonable supporting detail. Seller shall have thirty (30) days following receipt of the Earnout Statement to review it and deliver a written objection specifying in reasonable detail each disputed item and the basis for the objection. The Parties shall negotiate in good faith for twenty (20) Business Days after delivery of an objection. Any remaining dispute shall be submitted to an independent, nationally recognized accounting firm mutually agreed by the Parties, which shall act as an expert and not an arbitrator, resolve only the remaining disputed items, and issue a final and binding determination within thirty (30) days. The Independent Accountant shall not assign a value to any disputed item greater than the highest value or less than the lowest value claimed by either Party. Costs shall be allocated based on the relative success of the Parties’ positions.
>
> **(d) Operation of the Business During the Earnout Period.** Following the Closing, Buyer shall not, and shall cause the Company not to, take any action with the primary purpose of reducing or avoiding the Earnout Payment. For the avoidance of doubt, nothing in this Section 2.05(d) shall restrict Buyer’s right to operate, integrate, restructure, or otherwise manage the Company and its business in Buyer’s sole discretion, including the right to make capital expenditure decisions, change pricing, make personnel decisions, make strategic investments, acquire or dispose of businesses or assets, enter new markets, exit underperforming lines of business, allocate corporate overhead, make organizational changes, and modify operations. No such action shall constitute a breach of this Section 2.05(d) unless taken with the primary purpose of reducing or avoiding the Earnout Payment. Buyer shall have no obligation to maintain the Company as a separate entity, maintain any particular level of personnel, equipment, capital expenditures, customers, contracts, revenues, or business opportunities, or operate the Company in a manner consistent with past practice or designed to maximize the Earnout Payment.
>
> **(e) Payment of Earnout.** Any Earnout Payment finally determined to be payable pursuant to this Section 2.05 shall be paid by Buyer to Seller within sixty (60) days following the end of the Earnout Period, subject to final determination under Section 2.05(c), by wire transfer of immediately available funds. For U.S. federal income tax purposes, the Parties shall treat any Earnout Payment as an adjustment to the Purchase Price to the extent permitted by applicable Law.

### Track-changes comment

**[Buyer comment — CRITICAL: preserve platform-investment flexibility.]** The affirmative “past practice/maximize” covenant, resource-maintenance obligation, and anti-diversion language would constrain Buyer’s integration, restructuring, pricing, personnel, capital allocation, and bolt-on strategy through December 31, 2026. Strike the entire affirmative covenant and replace it with the agreed narrow primary-purpose negative covenant. The financial thresholds remain unchanged: $25,000,000 maximum; $38,000,000 full-payment threshold; $32,000,000 floor; linear interpolation; measurement period ending December 31, 2026. The Seller's 60-day statement and 10-Business-Day payment timing also do not track the term sheet's 45-day statement and 60-day payment framework.

**Sources:** Term Sheet §5; Playbook §§7.1–7.2 and checklist item 7; Partner Instructions ¶¶88–111; Delaware governing-law provision in Seller draft §10.02.

## 7. Section 2.03(d), Section 2.08, and Article VII — payoff letters and simultaneous debt payoff

**Priority: High**

### Seller's draft language

> “At or promptly following the Closing, Buyer shall cause the Company to repay, discharge, and satisfy in full all Closing Indebtedness. Seller shall use commercially reasonable efforts to cooperate with Buyer in connection with the repayment of such Closing Indebtedness.”

The Seller's draft does not require payoff letters three Business Days before Closing and does not make their delivery a Buyer closing condition.

### Proposed replacement language

Replace Section 2.03(d) with:

> **(d) Payoff Letters and Simultaneous Repayment of Closing Indebtedness.** Seller shall deliver, or cause to be delivered, to Buyer executed payoff letters from each holder of Closing Indebtedness, including Cascade Mutual Bank, Pacific Lease Corp., and Evergreen Holdings Group, Inc., no later than three (3) Business Days before the scheduled Closing Date. Each payoff letter shall state (i) the total amount required to repay the applicable Closing Indebtedness in full as of the Closing Date, including principal, accrued and unpaid interest, prepayment premiums, breakage costs, and all other amounts required to discharge the obligation; (ii) wire transfer instructions; and (iii) the holder’s irrevocable commitment to release all liens and security interests upon receipt of the payoff amount, including delivery of UCC-3 termination statements and other lien-release documents reasonably requested by Buyer or its financing sources. All Closing Indebtedness shall be repaid simultaneously at Closing through the funds flow, and no Closing Indebtedness shall remain outstanding after Closing. Buyer may direct the applicable payoff amounts to the holders in accordance with the payoff letters.

Add the following to Section 2.08(a) and Section 7.02:

> **Section 2.08(a)(x).** Executed payoff letters satisfying Section 2.03(d), together with all releases, UCC-3 termination statements, and other lien-release documents required to be delivered at Closing or held in escrow for automatic release upon payment.
>
> **Section 7.02(h).** All payoff letters required by Section 2.03(d) shall have been delivered to Buyer no later than three (3) Business Days before the Closing Date and shall remain in full force and effect as of Closing, and the applicable holders shall have committed to release all liens and security interests upon receipt of the payoff amounts.

### Track-changes comment

The term sheet makes payoff letters a binding closing mechanic. “At or promptly following” is not acceptable for Buyer or Clearwater Environmental Lending Corp. The revised language protects the cash-free/debt-free transaction structure and makes the $28,000,000 Cascade Mutual Bank loan, $9,800,000 Pacific Lease financing, and $4,500,000 Seller note part of the closing funds flow.

**Sources:** Term Sheet §6 and §18(vi); Playbook §9.2 and checklist item 9; Partner Instructions ¶¶193–205; Disclosure Schedule 4.13.

# ARTICLE IV — COMPANY REPRESENTATIONS

## 8. Section 4.16 — Government Contracts: novation/recognition representation

**Priority: Critical**

### Seller's draft language

> “Each Government Contract is in full force and effect and constitutes a legal, valid, and binding obligation of the Company and, to the Knowledge of the Company, of the applicable Governmental Authority. The Company is not in material breach or default under any Government Contract, and no event has occurred that, with the giving of notice or the lapse of time, or both, would constitute a material breach or default thereunder.”

### Proposed replacement language

Replace Section 4.16(b)–(d) with:

> **(b)** Each Government Contract is in full force and effect and constitutes a legal, valid, and binding obligation of the Company and, to the Knowledge of the Company, of the applicable Governmental Authority. The Company is not in material breach or default under any Government Contract, and no event has occurred that, with the giving of notice or the lapse of time, or both, would constitute a material breach or default thereunder.
>
> **(c)** No Government Contract is subject to any pending or threatened termination for default or convenience, suspension, non-renewal, material modification, cure notice, show-cause notice, adverse audit finding, or other proceeding or notice that would reasonably be expected to impair the Company’s rights or obligations under such Government Contract. The Company has not received written notice from any contracting officer or Governmental Authority indicating an intent to terminate, suspend, or materially modify any Government Contract as a result of the transactions contemplated by this Agreement.
>

> **(b) Non-Solicitation.** For a period of two (2) years following the Closing Date, Seller and its Affiliates shall not, directly or indirectly, solicit, recruit, hire, or engage any individual who is an employee of the Company as of the Closing Date, or induce, encourage, or attempt to induce or encourage any such employee to terminate employment with the Company; provided that this Section 6.09(b) shall not restrict (i) general solicitations of employment, including advertisements, job postings, or use of recruiting firms, that are not specifically directed at or targeted toward Company employees, or (ii) the hiring of any Company employee who contacts Seller or its Affiliates on the employee’s own initiative without solicitation by or on behalf of Seller or its Affiliates. For the avoidance of doubt, the non-solicitation covenant shall not prohibit general business communications with customers or suppliers that are not specifically directed at diverting such relationship from the Company.

### Track-changes comment

The five-year, nationwide, “any business” prohibition is inconsistent with the binding term sheet and would sweep in Evergreen's unrelated construction and timber operations. Narrow to three years, the four operating states, and the environmental remediation/hazardous waste management lines actually conducted by Cascadia. The draft's three-year employee/customer/supplier restriction also exceeds the term sheet's two-year employee-only covenant. The narrower language is more likely to be enforceable across the relevant jurisdictions.

**Sources:** Term Sheet §11 and §18(v); Playbook §10.1 and checklist item 10; Partner Instructions ¶¶237–246.

## 22. Section 10.05 — entire agreement / term sheet supersession

**Priority: Medium**

### Seller's draft language

> “This Agreement ... supersedes all prior and contemporaneous agreements ... including the letter of intent dated August 15, 2025 and the term sheet dated September 10, 2025 between Seller and Buyer.”

### Proposed replacement language

Replace the final phrase with:

> “... including the letter of intent dated August 15, 2025; provided, however, that this Agreement is intended to implement and be consistent with the Binding Term Sheet dated September 10, 2025, and nothing in this Agreement shall be construed to waive or supersede any economic or other binding term of that Binding Term Sheet unless this Agreement expressly states that such term is being modified.”

### Track-changes comment

The term sheet's binding provisions remain relevant to the markup because the draft presently contradicts several of them. The SPA should not create an argument that a seller-favorable draft silently superseded the agreed cap, Special Indemnity, payoff-letter mechanics, or non-compete parameters.

**Sources:** Term Sheet §2 (Definitive Agreement) and §18; Partner Instructions ¶¶25–40.

# ADDITIONAL MATERIAL ISSUES FOR PARTNER DISCUSSION

## 23. Diligence and disclosure-schedule inconsistencies — Dalton Creek

**Priority: High**

The DD Memo describes the EPA CERCLA §104(e) request as dated **February 12, 2025** and places Dalton Creek in **Clackamas County**, while Seller's Schedule 4.15(d), Schedule 4.19, and proposed Schedule 9.02(e) state **June 12, 2025** and **Lane County**. The memo also says “Clackamas County” in its background discussion, while the Seller disclosure uses “Lane County.” Before signing, confirm the correct date, county, regulatory file/reference number, and exact facility name. The Special Indemnity should cover the matter by site name and all related EPA correspondence, not depend on a potentially inconsistent date or county. Proposed clean-up language:

> “Dalton Creek Disposal Facility, Oregon (the ‘Dalton Creek Site’), including the facility identified in EPA’s CERCLA §104(e) information request to the Company dated June 12, 2025, or any successor, amended, reissued, or related request, regardless of the county designation or facility address used by EPA or any other Governmental Authority.”

**Sources:** DD Memo §§II–III and Schedule 4.15(d); Seller Disclosure Schedules 4.15(d), 4.19; Partner Instructions ¶¶279–281.

## 24. Fundamental Representation definition

**Priority: Medium**

Seller's definition includes Sections 3.01–3.03 and Company Sections 4.01–4.03 and 4.20, but omits Seller's no-conflicts representation in Section 3.04. Add Section 3.04:

> “ ‘Fundamental Representations’ means (a) the representations and warranties of Seller set forth in Sections 3.01, 3.02, 3.03, and 3.04, and (b) the representations and warranties regarding the Company set forth in Sections 4.01, 4.02, 4.03, and 4.20.”

The playbook identifies no-conflicts and brokers as core transaction representations; the term sheet also describes Seller's authority, title, and conflicts as Fundamental Representations.

## 25. Affiliate Lease closing treatment

**Priority: Medium**

The Seller's closing deliverables expressly carve out the Affiliate Lease from the requirement that Seller/affiliate contracts be terminated. Because the Affiliate Lease carries $1,600,000 of annual rent and is identified as an above-market EBITDA adjustment, Buyer should not leave its post-Closing treatment open. Add to Section 2.08(a)(vii):

> “The Affiliate Lease with Parkside Realty Holdings LLC shall have been terminated at or before Closing, or replaced with a new lease on terms, including rent, term, renewal rights, and termination rights, approved in writing by Buyer before Closing; provided that no replacement lease shall impose any obligation on Buyer or the Company beyond the Closing Date without Buyer’s written approval.”

If the business requires the premises, use a short-term interim lease on buyer-approved terms and document the fair-market rent adjustment in Exhibit D. This is a commercial decision for Marcus Devereaux and the client, but the current “addressed separately” language is incomplete.

## 26. Environmental escrow allocation

**Priority: High**

The draft provides a single $16,125,000 escrow and a 36-month hold only for pending Fundamental Representation claims. It should expressly allocate at least $1,500,000 to the Dalton Creek Special Indemnity, hold the Special Indemnity/environmental portion for 36 months, and state that Buyer can pursue Seller directly after the 36-month escrow release through the 72-month Special Indemnity survival period. The Escrow Agreement should be attached or finalized concurrently and should require joint instructions or a final, non-appealable court order/arbitration award for disputed releases.

## 27. Closing checklist — required deliverables to add

Before Buyer waives any closing condition, confirm delivery of:

- payoff letters from Cascade Mutual Bank, Pacific Lease Corp., and Evergreen Holdings Group, Inc. at least three Business Days before Closing;
- lien releases/UCC-3 termination statements or escrowed release documents;
- executed Patricia Huang employment agreement in Buyer-approved form, as already contemplated by the term sheet;
- R&W Insurance evidence and subrogation waiver;
- environmental permit change-of-control submissions and any required prior approvals;
- government-contract novation/recognition submissions and no-adverse-action confirmations;
- officer's certificate covering the revised environmental, government-contract, and permit covenants;
- evidence that the environmental insurance policies remain in force with no cancellation/non-renewal notice; and
- final confirmation of the correct Dalton Creek site, EPA request date, and regulatory reference.

# CONCLUSION

The first buyer markup should take a firm position on the Critical items: MAE qualifiers, cap conformity, pro-sandbagging, earnout operational flexibility, and Dalton Creek Special Indemnity. The High items—environmental survival, payoff mechanics, government-contract novation, affiliate transactions, environmental permit/operations covenants, and escrow coordination—should be included in the initial redline, not reserved for a later round. The Medium items—R&W subrogation, non-compete scope, environmental insurance drafting, Fundamental Representation definition, and Affiliate Lease treatment—are also draft-ready and should be addressed now because they are either term-sheet commitments or material diligence protections.

The only open strategic questions requiring client/partner direction are (i) whether to insist on completed government novations versus the proposed submission/no-denial closing condition, (ii) whether to move from the 36-month environmental survival minimum to full applicable limitations-period survival, and (iii) whether to require a separate Dalton Creek escrow or allocate at least $1,500,000 within the existing escrow. None of those questions justifies leaving the Seller's current omissions unmarked in the buyer's first draft.
"}
